item.title: Why all of Europe should be watching as Spain’s far-right Vox closes in on power | Eoghan Gilmartin
item.description:
Santiago Abascal’s party has adopted radical ideas from France and beyond. If it joins a PP coalition, it would be a morale boost for allies across the continent

It was a scene few would have imagined possible in Spanish politics until recently. Flanked on stage by Catalan flags, the far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, addressed a packed campaign rally in Girona, where he promised “to defend Catalan identity” against supposed “Islamisation”. He urged his audience to confront what he claimed was “the primary challenge” of a new “caliphate” across Spain. For a fringe party that made its breakthrough in 2018 by demonising Catalonia’s independence movement, it was a striking change of emphasis, reflecting a strategic shift that has brought Vox to the brink of power. When the results of this Sunday’s snap general election become clear, there is a strong likelihood that centre-left PM Pedro Sánchez will be forced out, with Vox as kingmakers and junior coalition partners to the traditionally dominant rightwing People’s party (PP).

The perpetually dour Abascal may lack the charisma of Trump or Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, but Vox is projected to increase its vote share from 12.4% in 2023 to close to 20%. It has achieved this surge not by moderating its rhetoric as it draws closer to power, but by embracing some of the most radical positions on immigration from across the European far right. A place in government for the party could, in turn, embolden its allies across Europe, as France, Italy and Poland prepare to go to the polls next year.

item.title: Thousands of girls and women report bleeding and miscarriages after French police use of teargas
item.description:
Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October give testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles

For three years, Naïma Di Piero says she barely had a period. The 46-year-old charity worker, who suffers from endometriosis, takes the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle. But two days after being exposed to police teargas during France’s nationwide protests on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily.

French police fired about 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters on 17 October at the height of the protests – equivalent to two grenades every three seconds (over 10 hours of maintaining order).

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv launched more long-range strikes in 2026 than rest of war combined, data shows
item.description:
Ukrainian strikes on targets more than 500km away increased, with Siberia and Libya among the locations hit. What we know on day 1,738

Ukraine launched nearly 500 strikes at Russian targets more than 500km away in 2026 – more than in the first four years of the war combined, according to data from the ACLED conflict monitor. Most of the attacks hit Russian territory, with Ukrainian drones reaching Moscow, St Petersburg and as far away as Siberia, and AFP analysis of ACLED’s figures up to 20 November showed. Some targets were as far as 1,500km away from both sides, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claiming strikes on two vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday that sank a Russian warship. As early as December 2025, ACLED recorded a strike by Kyiv in the Mediterranean, near the Greek and Libyan coasts, on an oil tanker from Russia’s “shadow fleet”. It said the incident was considered the first attack of its kind in the area since the start of the war.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha expressed “regret” over the “unintended consequences” of a Ukrainian attack on Russian ships in the Libyan port of Benghazi, saying it was directed at Moscow, not at Libya. After speaking ⁠to his Libyan counterpart, Sybiha, writing on X, said Ukraine had no intention of extending the war against Russia to Libya or ⁠any other country. Ukraine says it sank the Russian naval corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday because they were transporting military equipment. But the attack, which killed two ⁠Libyan army personnel, was condemned by Libya’s ​western-backed government of national unity based in Tripoli, and by the eastern-based ‌Libyan National ‌Army (LNA) General Command, which has ties with Russia.

US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to “pull back all military aggression” against Europe, in another shift in tone towards the Russian leader. Trump said he thought it would help lead to a deal to end the war in Ukraine. The statement – which did not specify which territories Trump meant and did not specifically include Ukraine – comes a day after Trump hosted Nato chief Mark Rutte in Florida, where the two leaders called on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war. “During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

Zelenskyy on Thursday said Ukraine had information that Russia was planning a ⁠big attack on ⁠the ​country in the coming days. “Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass ⁠strike being prepared by the Russians,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address. “In the coming ⁠days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats. ​And in Russia, ‌they should know ‌that we will rebuild what is ours and retaliate ‌against every Russian strike.” The warning was the second issued by the president this week.

Ukrainian military intelligence said Ukrainian drones had struck an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar ⁠region, and oil ​reservoirs at Russia’s ​Transneft oil facility in ​the central Bashkortostan region overnight. The ​Marinovka military ‌airfield in the Volgograd ​region was hit also. A drone attack claimed by Ukraine on Thursday set a major Russian refinery on fire and caused serious damage, the owner said, weeks after a previous strike forced a halt to its production.

EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year. Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said. Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan.
